A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CS-Bench. Their main text, figures, tables, equation, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite additions, reordering, and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM evaluations, prompting experiments, error analyses, scaling fits, and human–GPT-4 scoring agreement, including English and Chinese appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds multilingual evaluations, newer models, judge comparisons, representation analyses, and retrieval, tool-use, and fine-tuning experiments.

M1.justification: v2 Appendix E.6 adds implemented inference and training adaptations: extracting keywords, retrieving and summarizing Wikipedia information for context; executing generated Python code and feeding results back to the model; and supervised fine-tuning on CS-Bench data. These substantially extend the procedures investigated beyond v1's prompting and existing expert models, while retaining the core benchmark scoring scheme.

E1.justification: CS-Bench expands from English and Chinese with 4,838 samples to four languages with 9,676 samples, adding French and German evaluations in v2 Figure 17. The four CS domains and task formats remain. Figure 9 and Appendix E.5 also extend the analysis to tool-use, long-context, general-chat, and non-CS science benchmarks; Figure 9 uses externally reported scores rather than claiming new evaluations on those benchmarks.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds Mistral-Large-123B, Llama3.1-405B, and Claude-3.5-Sonnet. Figure 4 and Table 14 add o1-mini and o1-preview comparisons. Appendix D.2 introduces a comparison crossing four Claude variants as tested models and judges, alongside GPT-4 scoring. The earlier Claude-3 entry is retained as Claude-3-Opus, not newly added.

E3.justification: The main validation/test split and scoring protocols remain. New experiments introduce crossed judge/test-model evaluation, reasoning and completion-token measurements, pooled hidden-state cosine-distance comparisons, and retrieval/tool-assisted conditions. Appendix E.6 additionally uses a distinct fine-tuning design: 10% of English CS-Bench becomes a mini-test set and the remaining data becomes training data.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained prompting, scaling, and error analyses, v2 adds judge-sensitivity tests in Appendix D.2, comparisons testing the specificity of CS–math/code correlations in Figure 9, representation analyses in E.5, intervention experiments in E.6, and three o1 case studies in E.7. These address substantial new questions about evaluation robustness, capability relationships, and improvement mechanisms.

E5.justification: Both versions document three-run averaging in Appendix D.3. Appendix D.2 retains three human raters, 100 examples per generative task, Cronbach's alpha, and Pearson agreement. v2 introduces no revised repetition counts, seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures; additional correlation results do not change the uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Matched original English, Chinese, and subfield table entries remain unchanged. Added results include o1-mini and o1-preview overall scores of 77.06% and 82.65%, plus multilingual, judge, correlation, and representation findings. Appendix E.6 reports Llama3-8B improving from 54.37% to 60.47% with retrieval, and from 58.07% to 63.07% with fine-tuning on the separate mini-test. The latter is not a main-test performance comparison.

T1.justification: Appendix E.2 retains Equation 1, its monotonicity and limiting-behavior requirements, and the fitting rationale. The new representation, intervention, and token-consumption analyses do not introduce new theoretical propositions, proofs, or substantive revisions to the existing mathematics.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement broaden the benchmark claim from approximately 5K bilingual samples to approximately 10K samples in four languages. The introduction and conclusion extend the challenge claim to o1. The central contributions—a dedicated CS benchmark, scaling and error findings, and CS–math/code relationships—remain the same.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking capability correlations to representations and data characteristics, interpretations of judge capability and scoring fairness, and implications of retrieval, symbolic tools, and fine-tuning. Section 3.3 discusses performance–token-cost tradeoffs. Appendix A expands the existing coverage caveats with explicit difficulty/task biases, their effects on discrimination, and the rationale for excluding programming questions.

D1.justification: Appendix C.1 newly documents OCR, manual cross-checking, and additional source examples; D.2 clarifies raters' qualifications and shared scoring criteria. E.5–E.6 describe representation extraction and intervention implementation, although detailed fine-tuning settings remain unspecified. Existing hardware and inference hyperparameters are retained. The abstract replaces v1's direct data/code repository pointer with the project homepage, without establishing that resource availability changed.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for newer models, benchmarks such as GPQA, T-Eval, L-eval, BBH, and Chatbot Arena, and safety work including HarmBench, SEAS, and SG-Bench. Section 4 retains the same main positioning against broad multidisciplinary benchmarks and application-specific CS research. The switch to author–date citations is a presentation change.

P1.justification: v2 revises the opening motivation and selected explanations, inserts a dedicated o1 section, expands appendix organization, and adds acknowledgements. Publication headers, corresponding-author information, and citation style change. Most original paragraphs and the overall narrative sequence remain, so the revision is not an extensive rewrite of the retained material.

P2.justification: v2 adds token-cost displays, cross-benchmark correlations, multilingual comparisons, representation plots, and judge/intervention/case-study tables. Existing leaderboards and radar plots expand their axes and legends, and the math/code comparison plots reorder models. Dataset displays and multilingual examples expand, while v1's Chinese word-length figure is removed. The conference template also changes typography and page layout.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence behind v1's diagnoses and recommendations: Appendix D.2 tests sensitivity to the scoring model, Figure 9 adds comparisons beyond math/code, and Appendix E.6 directly tests retrieval, symbolic tools, and domain fine-tuning. Multilingual and o1 evaluations broaden applicability and expose inference-cost tradeoffs. These are substantive validation gains. Some additions remain imperfect: fine-tuning details are sparse, and Table 30 labels o1-preview successful despite an incorrect leaf count. Those localized weaknesses do not outweigh the stronger empirical support.
